No more than two subzones for housing are allowed in any particular zone. No more than one retail subzone is allowed in any zone in which a subzone is designated for housing. Industrial subzones are not allowed in any zone in which a subzone is designated for housing or three subzones are designated for retail use.
question: If three subzones are designated for each use, then which one of the following is allowed?
options: A) Exactly one subzone in Z3 is designated for industrial use and exactly one subzone in Z3 is designated for retail use.
B) Exactly two subzones in Z2 are designated for housing.
C) Three subzones in Z1 are designated for industrial use.
D) Three subzones in Z2 are designated for industrial use and exactly one subzone in Z2 is designated for retail use.
E) Three subzones in Z3 are designated for retail use.
raw_output:
Let's analyze the Millville situation step‐by‐step. There are three zones (Z1, Z2, Z3) and three types of subzones: housing, industrial, and retail. Overall, exactly three subzones are assigned of each use. In addition, the following restrictions hold:

1. There may be no retail subzones in Z1.
2. In any one zone, at most two subzones may be designated for housing.
3. If a zone has any housing, then it may have at most one retail subzone.
4. If a zone has even one industrial subzone then it cannot have any housing subzone.
5. Also, if a zone has three retail subzones then industrial subzones are not allowed there.

Now let’s work through each option quickly to see which one can be part of an overall assignment that meets the totals and these rules.

──────────────────────────────
Option A: “Exactly one subzone in Z3 is designated for industrial use and exactly one subzone in Z3 is designated for retail use.”

• In Z3 this forces industrial = 1 and retail = 1. Because there’s an industrial subzone in Z3, no housing can be assigned there.
• This means all 3 housing subzones must be in Z1 and Z2. However, note that Z1 cannot have retail at all (by rule) and any zone that gets housing may not get any industrial.
• Thus, we’d have to “split” the three housing subzones between Z1 and Z2 and, simultaneously, locate the remaining 2 industrial subzones in whichever zone(s) do not have housing. But then one of Z1 or Z2 would have to carry both housing and industrial – which is not allowed—and also Z1 cannot have retail.
• A careful check shows no valid overall assignment can be made.

──────────────────────────────
Option B: “Exactly two subzones in Z2 are designated for housing.”

Let’s see if we can build an assignment with this condition.

• In Z2, set housing = 2. Because housing is present in Z2, Z2 may have at most one retail subzone and no industrial subzones.
• Since overall housing must total 3, the remaining 1 housing subzone must be placed in either Z1 or Z3. (Remember, each zone with housing forbids industrial.)
• Notice Z1 cannot have retail and, if we assign housing to Z1 then no industrial can be in Z1. So let’s try:
  – Z1: housing = 1, industrial = 0, retail = 0.
  – Z2: housing = 2, industrial = 0, and we can assign up to 1 retail here. Let’s give Z2 retail = 1.
• Now, to meet the overall totals: 
  – Total housing now is 1 (Z1) + 2 (Z2) + 0 (Z3) = 3.
  – Total retail needed is 3; with 0 in Z1 and 1 in Z2 we need 2 in Z3.
  – Total industrial needed is 3; since neither Z1 nor Z2 can have industrial (because they have housing) all 3 industrial subzones must be assigned to Z3.
• Check Z3: Z3 would get industrial = 3 and retail = 2. In Z3 there is no housing so having both industrial and retail is allowed provided that retail is not 3 (the rule with “three retail” only affects industrial if there are 3 retail subzones). Here retail is 2, so that’s acceptable.
• All rules are obeyed:
  – Z1 has no retail (good),
  – Zones with housing (Z1 and Z2) do not have any industrial,
  – Zone Z2, which has housing, has at most one retail,
  – Z3 (an industrial zone) has no housing and its retail count is less than 3.
• Thus a complete assignment satisfying all totals and restrictions is possible under Option B.

──────────────────────────────
Option C: “Three subzones in Z1 are designated for industrial use.”

• If Z1 has industrial = 3 then by rule Z1 cannot have housing. Z1 already is barred from retail, so Z1 would contribute 0 housing and 0 retail.
• Then in zones Z2 and Z3 we must supply all 3 housing subzones. But note that each zone may have at most 2 housing subzones. Even by allocating 2 in one and 1 in the other, placing any housing in a zone prevents that zone from holding industrial.
• In that case, with no industrial allowed in Z2 or Z3 (as soon as they get housing), we can’t reach the overall industrial total of 3 because all 3 industrial are in Z1. In fact, if we try to reassign, we find that the assignment forced by a “3 industrial in Z1” ultimately pushes retail totals out of balance.
• So Option C cannot work.

──────────────────────────────
Option D: “Three subzones in Z2 are designated for industrial use and exactly one subzone in Z2 is designated for retail use.”

• In Z2, if industrial = 3 then no housing can be in Z2.
• With overall housing = 3, the housing must all come from Z1 and Z3. However, Z1 can have no retail, so retail must come from Z3 in order to reach total retail = 3.
• But if Z3 supplies all retail (3) then by rule no industrial can be present in Z3.
• Moreover, if Z1 contains housing then it cannot have industrial either.
• Then the required industrial total of 3 would be coming solely from Z2 (which already has 3 assigned) – that seems fine for industrial, but then consider the retail totals: Z2 provides 1 and Z3 must provide 2. However, if Z3 also has housing (to sum to 3 with Z1) then its retail would be limited to 1.
• No distribution among Z1 and Z3 can meet both the housing (which must total 3 with a maximum of 2 per zone) and the retail totals simultaneously.
• Hence Option D fails.

──────────────────────────────
Option E: “Three subzones in Z3 are designated for retail use.”

• In Z3, if retail = 3 then by the rule about industrial in zones with three retail subzones, no industrial subzones can be in Z3.
• Also, if housing were placed in Z3 together with three retail subzones, it would violate the rule that in any zone with housing only one retail is allowed.
• Thus Z3 must have neither housing nor industrial.
• This forces all 3 housing subzones to fall into Z1 and Z2. However, Z1 already is banned from retail and if either Z1 or Z2 receives housing then that zone cannot have any industrial subzones.
• With overall industrial needing to be 3 and no industrial allowed in Z3 (by the three retail rule) or in any zone with housing, it becomes impossible to assign the industrial subzones.
• So Option E fails.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Only Option B can be part of an overall assignment that meets all the given conditions. 

The correct answer is B.

Thus, with one industrial already in each zone, no housing is allowed anywhere and Z1 cannot have retail. The only variability remaining is in zones Z2 and Z3 where any extra subzones (beyond the required industrial one) must be retail and their total number across zones cannot exceed three.

Now let’s examine the answer options given the conditions:

Option A: “More subzones are designated for retail use in Z2 than in Z3.”

  • Z1: 1 subzone (industrial only).
  • Z2: 1 industrial + 1 retail (total = 2).
  • Z3: 1 industrial + 0 retail (total = 1).

Option B states that “A subzone in one of the zones is designated for housing.”
